messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night the tornado hit, Elias was twenty years old, sleeping in a second-floor apartment that offered little protection against the storm. One moment he was dreaming, and the next, the structural groan of collapsing timber drowned out the sirens. He spent hours wedged in the dark between a fallen wall and his mattress, breathing a thick mixture of wet ash, shattered insulation, and damp plaster. When rescuers cut him free, Elias walked away unharmed, but the specific violence of the event—the sudden collapse of his safe space and the suffocating scent that clung to his clothes—left a visceral imprint. That exact sensory profile now surfaces whenever he works the grill at his fast-food job; the sharp tang of frying oil and the sudden clatter of metal trays instantly trigger the smell of wet ash and bring back the same terror he felt trapped in the rubble. For Elias, remembering the event brings back the same terror he felt at the time, and his memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images. These visual fragments—twisted rebar, glittering glass—do not pass as gentle recollections. Instead, they flood his mind with such intensity that they directly shape his self-view, convincing him that the person he has become is unrecognisable to him. He looks in the mirror and no longer sees the friend he was, because the recurring terror and vivid scenes make him feel as though his core identity was shattered. He is certain he lost his happiness completely, interpreting these inescapable flashes as proof that he used to be a happy person but now is always miserable. Because Elias believes he has permanently changed for the worse, the intrusions themselves become far more threatening. His conviction that he is fundamentally broken acts as a lens that amplifies the visual memories, forcing him to stare at them with dread. This appraisal of permanent damage makes the terror on recall feel like a predictive warning that his mind is failing, which ensures that the olfactory recall of damp plaster and ash returns with greater force whenever a trigger appears. He cannot dismiss the flashbacks as harmless echoes; his negative self-judgment fuels their intensity, guaranteeing the memories will dominate his attention. Believing he is permanently damaged and emotionally hollow, Elias adopts rigid habits to keep the world at a distance. His conviction that he is unrecognisable directly leads him to avoid anything that could be stressful, a rule he enforces by declining weekend plans and stepping back from college. At work, this avoidance manifests as a refusal to take the lunch rush, which strains his standing but feels necessary to prevent panic. The belief that he has permanently changed also compels him to suppress thoughts, forcing him to immediately divert his focus to mundane tasks whenever the trauma tries to surface. He treats his mind like a sealed room, convinced any unguarded moment will invite the same overwhelming dread. These maneuvers only cement his bleak self-perception. By rehearsing what to say before any interaction, Elias strips every relationship of spontaneity, leaving him isolated and confirming his fear that he is permanently changed for the worse. The more he avoids stressors and suppresses his thoughts, the more stagnant his life becomes, turning his avoidance into undeniable proof of his unrecognisable self. He notices how his rehearsed scripts drain his energy, yet he clings to them because he is certain his core has been irrevocably damaged. Now, Elias sits in a clinic waiting room with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, the rhythmic hum of the air conditioner making his chest tighten. He has finally come to this appointment because his latest supervisor warning crossed a line he could no longer rationalize, and because the constant mental rehearsal has left him hollowed out. What he is most hoping for is a return to the person he remembers, a belief that the permanent damage he fears is not truly final, and a way to step back into a world that no longer feels like a series of threats waiting to collapse.
